editorialCapacity.reason: The Stockholm site has a wide, internally coherent collection spanning paintings and sculpture, applied arts and design, and prints and drawings, with a strong Swedish and Nordic emphasis. Twenty works would not adequately represent those media and the museum's collection logic; forty allows a substantial core route plus works that explain the design/applied-arts and graphic-arts identities. Sixty is not justified for this run because the scope is one primary visitor building rather than a Louvre-scale, cross-civilisation museum network.
editorialCapacity.planningBoundary: Capacity applies to the Stockholm Nationalmuseum building and its permanent collection presentation, not to the institution's dispersed external venues or temporary exhibitions.

includedSite.name: Nationalmuseum Stockholm main building
includedSite.boundary: The visitor-facing Nationalmuseum site on Blasieholmen, including the permanent collection displays and on-site sculpture courtyards. Online collection records may enter the downstream candidate pool only when later research verifies their relevance and visitor-facing status for this site.

collectionGroups.name: Paintings and sculptures
collectionGroups.scope: Paintings and sculpture from the late Middle Ages/Renaissance through around 1900, including Swedish, Dutch, French and other European holdings described by the museum.
collectionGroups.candidateCondition: Include as a collection family; each later candidate must be tied to a unique official object record and its display or access status must be verified downstream.

collectionGroups.name: Design and applied arts
collectionGroups.scope: Applied arts, design and industrial design from the late Middle Ages/14th century through the present, including ceramics, textiles, glass, metalwork, furniture and books, with priority given by the museum to Sweden and the Nordic countries.
collectionGroups.candidateCondition: Include the Stockholm-displayed collection family; treat the separately located Gustavsberg collection and museum as an exclusion below.

collectionGroups.name: Prints and drawings
collectionGroups.site: Nationalmuseum collection administered from Stockholm; visitor visibility to be verified per object
collectionGroups.scope: Prints and drawings from the late Middle Ages to 1900, including the Tessin master-drawing holdings and other named graphic-art strengths.
collectionGroups.candidateCondition: Include as a research family, but do not assume that an online record is currently on display; downstream research must verify access, display or an explicitly usable museum presentation.

collectionBoundaries.institutionalContext: Nationalmuseum is both Sweden's museum of art and design and a government authority. Its collections are broader than the Stockholm building, so institutional administration is not by itself sufficient to include an external venue in this run.

exclusions.name: Gustavsberg Porcelain Museum and the Gustavsberg collection
exclusions.reason: Separate museum and location; although part of Nationalmuseum institutionally and covered by some Nationalmuseum admission products, it is not part of the Stockholm Blasieholmen visit boundary.

exclusions.name: National Portrait Gallery at Gripsholm Castle and other Royal Castles collections
exclusions.reason: The portrait gallery and royal-castle holdings are displayed at separate castles outside the Stockholm main building and require a separate destination decision.

exclusions.name: The Tessin Institute's art collection and its displays at the Swedish Institute in Paris
exclusions.reason: Separate institution/venue in Paris; administered by Nationalmuseum but outside a Stockholm museum visit.

exclusions.name: Other external Nationalmuseum venues, including Jamtli and Läckö Castle
exclusions.reason: Separate venues outside the defined Stockholm site boundary; excluded from this single-site scope.

exclusions.name: Temporary exhibitions
exclusions.reason: Excluded from the stable collection scope even when exhibited in the main building or included in admission, because this stage establishes the enduring collection boundary rather than a date-specific exhibition programme.
